docs.title: AceUnit
docs.text:
Advanced C and Embedded Unit Test Framework

AceUnit is a comfortable, portable unit test framework for C — in the best tradition of xUnit frameworks like JUnit 5. Its target audience: developers writing firmware, drivers, operating systems, and other C programs who want test discovery without framework noise.

#include <aceunit.h>

void testLeapYears(void) {
    assert(isLeapYear(0));
    assert(isLeapYear(4));
    assert(isLeapYear(400));
}

void testNonLeapYears(void) {
    assert(!isLeapYear(1));
    assert(!isLeapYear(100));
}

Run it:

AceUnit: 2 test cases, 2 successful, 0 failed.

No registration macros. No test lists to maintain. AceUnit discovers tests automatically from object files.

docs.title: Why AceUnit?
docs.text: Feature AceUnit Check Unity CUnit Test discovery (no registration) ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ No macro noise in test code ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ Freestanding / bare-metal support ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗ C89 through C23 ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗ Multiple runners (simple/setjmp/abort/fork) ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ No Java / external toolchain needed ✓ (shell script) ✓ ✓ ✓

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• JUnit 5-style naming — beforeAll, beforeEach, test*, afterEach, afterAll
  • Automatic test discovery — no REGISTER_TEST macros; aceunit reads object files via nm/objdump/readelf
  • Tiny footprint — suitable for extremely resource-constrained environments
  • Four runners — Simple, SetJmp, Abort, Fork; pick what fits your environment
  • C89–C23 — works with ancient compilers on ancient hardware
  • Broad compiler support — GCC, Clang, Keil, and more
  • POSIX and bare-metal — same tests, different runner

docs.title: Quick Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/christianhujer/aceunit
cd aceunit
make
sudo make install

Then get started →

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
Include one header:

#include <aceunit.h>

docs.title: aceunit_func_t
docs.text:
typedef void (*aceunit_func_t)(void);

Function pointer type used for test cases and lifecycle functions.

docs.title: AceUnit_Fixture_t
docs.text:
typedef struct {
    const aceunit_func_t beforeAll;
    const aceunit_func_t afterAll;
    const aceunit_func_t beforeEach;
    const aceunit_func_t afterEach;
    const aceunit_func_t *testcases;
} AceUnit_Fixture_t;

Describes a single fixture (object file). Usually auto-generated by aceunit.

Field Description beforeAll Called once before any test case; NULL if absent afterAll Called once after all test cases; NULL if absent beforeEach Called before each test case; NULL if absent afterEach Called after each test case; NULL if absent testcases NULL-terminated array of test case function pointers

docs.title: AceUnit_Result_t
docs.text:
typedef struct {
    int testCaseCount;
    int successCount;
    int failureCount;
} AceUnit_Result_t;

Accumulates results across one or more runs.

Note

AceUnit_run() does not initialize result. Zero-initialize it before the first call so multiple runs can be collected into the same result.

docs.title: AceUnit_run()
docs.text:
void AceUnit_run(const AceUnit_Fixture_t *fixtures[], AceUnit_Result_t *result);

Runs all fixtures in fixtures and accumulates results into *result.

  • fixtures — NULL-terminated array of fixture pointers; must not be NULL
  • result — output; must not be NULL; must be initialized by caller

docs.title: runCatching()
docs.text:
bool runCatching(void(*code)(void));

Calls code, catching failures according to the linked runner's implementation.

Returns true on success, false on failure. Implementations may also not return at all (e.g., SimpleRunner calling abort()).

docs.title: AceUnit_fail()
docs.text:
void AceUnit_fail(void);

Fails and aborts the current test case. The mechanism depends on the linked runner:

Runner Mechanism Simple abort() SetJmp longjmp() Abort abort() (caught via SIGABRT handler) Fork abort() (child process terminates)

docs.title: assert()
docs.text:
#define assert(cond)

Defined by <aceunit.h> if <assert.h> has not already defined it. Calls AceUnit_fail() when cond is false. On hosted environments, also prints the failing expression, file, and line to stderr.

docs.title: fixtures[]
docs.text:
extern const AceUnit_Fixture_t *fixtures[];

The global NULL-terminated fixture array, referenced by the generated main(). Auto-generated by aceunit and compiled from testcases.c.

docs.title: main()
docs.text:
int main(int argc, const char *argv[]);

Provided by the AceUnit library. Calls AceUnit_run(fixtures, &result) and prints a summary. Requires fixtures to be defined (by compiling the aceunit-generated testcases.c).

docs.title: __wrap_main()
docs.text:
int __wrap_main(int argc, const char *argv[]);

Alternative entry point for programs that already have a main(). Link with --wrap=main (or -Wl,--wrap=main) to redirect main to __wrap_main while still keeping the original main accessible via __real_main.

cc *.o testcases.o -laceunit-fork -Wl,--wrap=main -o tests

docs.title: How Assertions Work
docs.text:
AceUnit tests fail by calling AceUnit_fail(). The assert() macro provided by <aceunit.h> calls it automatically when a condition is false.

#include <aceunit.h>

void testSomething(void) {
    assert(1 + 1 == 2);   // passes
    assert(1 + 1 == 3);   // calls AceUnit_fail()
}

On a hosted environment, assert() also prints the failing condition and location to stderr before failing.

docs.title: Assertion vs Runner Compatibility
docs.text:
Not every assertion mechanism works with every runner. This table shows what each runner supports:

Assertion SimpleRunner SetJmpRunner AbortRunner ForkRunner <aceunit.h> assert() stop ✓ ✓ ✓ <assert.h> assert() stop ✗ ✓ ✓ <stdlib.h> abort() stop ✗ ✓ ✓ <stdlib.h> exit() stop ✗ ✗ ✓ <setjmp.h> longjmp() ✗ ✓ ✓ ✗ Abnormal termination (SIGSEGV, etc.) ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓

Legend:

  • ✓ — Runner catches this; test is marked failed and execution continues.
  • stop — Runner detects failure but does not continue to next test case.
  • ✗ — Runner does not handle this; test execution aborts entirely.

docs.title: Choosing the Right Assertion Style
docs.text:
Embedded / freestanding with setjmp.h: Use <aceunit.h> assert with SetJmpRunner. longjmp() provides the non-local exit.

Hosted POSIX: Use <assert.h> with ForkRunner. Each test case runs in a child process; even SIGSEGV is caught.

Hosted non-POSIX (Windows, AmigaOS, MS-DOS): Use AbortRunner. SIGABRT is caught via a signal handler.

Quick start / learning TDD: SimpleRunner works fine. It stops on first failure, which is acceptable early on.

docs.title: AceUnit_fail()
docs.text:
You can call AceUnit_fail() directly to fail a test case unconditionally:

void testUnreachable(void) {
    if (should_not_happen()) {
        AceUnit_fail();
    }
}

The exact mechanism used by AceUnit_fail() depends on the linked runner library:

  • libaceunit-simple.a — calls abort()
  • libaceunit-setjmp.a — calls longjmp()
  • libaceunit-abort.a — calls abort() (caught by signal handler)
  • libaceunit-fork.a — calls abort() (caught via child process exit status)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
aceunit [OPTION]... [OBJECT_FILE]...

Scans object files for test cases and writes the generated fixtures table to stdout.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: -b BINARY Use BINARY instead of the default binary for the selected tool. Example: -b m68k-amigaos-objdump -h Display help text and exit. -n NAME Use NAME instead of fixtures as the symbol name for the fixture table. -p PATTERN Match test functions with the prefix PATTERN. PATTERN is passed to grep. Example: -p '[^_\+]_' to allow any module prefix followed by an underscore. -s PATTERN Strip PATTERN from symbol names before processing. PATTERN is passed to grep. Example: -s _ to strip a leading underscore (needed for some toolchains like bcc). -t TOOL Use TOOL to display symbol tables. Defaults to objdump. Built-in options: nm, objdump, readelf. -v Print version information and exit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Scan all test object files and write fixtures to aceunit.c:

aceunit -p '[^_]\+_' *_test.o >aceunit.c

Use nm with a cross-compiler binary, stripping leading underscores:

aceunit -t nm -b m68k-amigaos-nm -s _ *_test.o >aceunit.c

Use readelf with explicit object files:

aceunit -t readelf a.o b.o c.o >aceunit.c

For bcc (Bruce's C Compiler) targeting x86-DOS:

aceunit -t nm -b nm86 -s _ *_test.o >aceunit.c

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: aceunit requires one of: objdump, readelf, or nm.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: aceunit cannot read from stdin. This is a limitation of the downstream tools (nm, objdump, readelf) which require actual file paths.

docs.title: Shell Compatibility
docs.text: The aceunit script requires bash 5, ksh, or zsh. On macOS, the system bash at /bin/bash is too old. Run ./configure.sh to switch to zsh, or install a newer bash via Homebrew.

docs.title: Fixtures
docs.text:
A fixture is an object file (.o) that contains test cases and optionally lifecycle functions. AceUnit scans fixtures using aceunit to generate a fixture table.

There is no special source-level annotation. AceUnit uses naming conventions and reads the object file's symbol table.

docs.title: Test Cases
docs.text:
A test case is any function whose name starts with test (or a user-defined prefix). It takes no arguments and returns void.

void testAddition(void) {
    assert(add(1, 2) == 3);
}

AceUnit runs all such functions in the fixture, in the order they appear in the symbol table.

docs.title: Lifecycle Functions
docs.text:
Each fixture may define at most one of each lifecycle function:

Function When called Count beforeAll() Once before any test case in the fixture 0 or 1 beforeEach() Before every test case 0 or 1 afterEach() After every test case 0 or 1 afterAll() Once after all test cases in the fixture 0 or 1 
static int counter;

void beforeAll(void) { counter = 0; }

void beforeEach(void) { reset_state(); }

void testOne(void) { assert(counter++ == 0); }

void afterEach(void) { cleanup(); }

void afterAll(void) { assert(counter == 1); }

docs.title: Test Discovery
docs.text:
aceunit scans object files for symbols matching the lifecycle and test naming conventions. It generates a C source file with a fixture table — no manual registration required.

aceunit leapyear_test.o >testcases.c

The generated testcases.c contains an array of AceUnit_Fixture_t structures and a main() that runs them.

docs.title: Custom Prefixes
docs.text:
If your project uses a naming convention with a module prefix, you can tell aceunit about it:

aceunit -p 'HeapTest_' heap_test.o >testcases.c

This discovers functions like HeapTest_beforeAll, HeapTest_test_allocate, etc.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: AfterAll A function AceUnit runs once after all test cases in a fixture. AfterEach A function AceUnit runs after each test case. Assertion Code that verifies an expectation; calls AceUnit_fail() on failure. BeforeAll A function AceUnit runs once before any test case in a fixture. BeforeEach A function AceUnit runs before each test case. Fixture An object file containing test cases and optional lifecycle functions. Runner The part of AceUnit that executes test functions. See Runners. Test Case A function AceUnit executes as a test. Test Function Any of: beforeAll, beforeEach, test case, afterEach, afterAll.

docs.title: General Guidelines
docs.text:
• Follow the Code of Conduct.
  • Make sure you are allowed to contribute. If you are employed and unsure, check with your employer or a lawyer.
  • Make sure you understand and accept the License.

docs.title: Quality Standards
docs.text:
No regressions. AceUnit has an extensive test suite. Run make before submitting a PR and ensure all tests pass.

Bug fixes require a reproducing test. Write a failing test that demonstrates the bug, then fix it.

New features must be tested. TDD is the expected workflow.

Code style: 1TBS with 4-space indentation, Unix line endings.

  • No tabs in C files (tabs are fine in Makefile recipes)
  • No CRLF
  • Curly braces open at end of line ({ on the same line as if, for, function signature)

Follow the SEI CERT C Coding Standard.

If you are unsure about any quality requirement, submit the PR anyway. You will receive guidance.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/christianhujer/aceunit
cd aceunit
make        # build and run all tests

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
make        # builds everything and runs tests
make test   # runs tests only (if already built)

docs.title: Cross-Compilation Tests
docs.text:
To run the cross-hosted test suite (requires clang and qemu):

cd test/cross-hosted
make

docs.title: Reporting Bugs
docs.text: Open an issue at: https://github.com/christianhujer/aceunit/issues

docs.title: Security Issues
docs.text: AceUnit is a development-only tool and is not intended to be shipped in production systems. If you find a security vulnerability, treat it as a bug and report it via the issue tracker. See SECURITY.md for details.

docs.title: Cross-Compilation
docs.text: AceUnit supports cross-compiling and testing for multiple target architectures. This is useful when your embedded target has different alignment, endianness, or word size than your development machine.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• clang (supports many targets without separate toolchain installs)
  • qemu-user (to run cross-compiled binaries)
  • GCC cross-compiler packages for specific targets

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The Makefile in lib/ is designed to be invoked from other directories. You pass CC=<cross-compiler> to build and test for a different target.

make CC=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc

The test/cross-hosted/ directory shows this pattern fully.

docs.title: Known Broken Targets
docs.text:
The following targets are excluded from the default cross-compilation suite:

Target Reason avr Compiles but no qemu-user support hppa64-linux-gnu Known broken (qemu/gcc bug) m68k-linux-gnu Known broken (qemu/gcc bug) sh4-linux-gnu Needs investigation sparc64-linux-gnu Known broken (qemu/gcc bug)

When using CC=clang, additional targets are excluded:

Target Reason alpha-linux-gnu Clang does not support Alpha AXP hppa-linux-gnu Clang does not support HP/PA-RISC hppa64-linux-gnu Clang does not support HP/PA-RISC 64-bit sh4-linux-gnu Clang does not support SH4

m68k on Ubuntu

m68k is supported in Clang/LLVM 13 and 15 but not in Clang/LLVM 14 on Ubuntu.

docs.title: Example: Testing for Multiple Targets in Parallel
docs.text:
cd test/cross-hosted
make                    # GCC default targets
make CC=clang           # Clang targets

docs.title: Using AceUnit in a Cross-Compilation Project
docs.text:
When testing firmware for an embedded target, you typically run the tests on the host machine (not on the target). The key is to build your production code for the target and your test code for the host, then link against the host AceUnit library.

Pattern:

CROSS_CC=arm-none-eabi-gcc
HOST_CC=gcc

# Build production code for target
module.target.o: module.c
    $(CROSS_CC) -c $< -o $@

# Build test code for host
module_test.o: module_test.c
    $(HOST_CC) -I$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/include -c $< -o $@

# Generate and run tests on host
testcases.c: module_test.o
    $(ACEUNIT_HOME)/bin/aceunit $^ >$@

module_test: module.o module_test.o testcases.o
    $(HOST_CC) $^ -L$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/lib -laceunit-fork -o $@

This tests your C logic on the host while building the final firmware for the target.

docs.title: "declare: -g: invalid option"
docs.text:
./aceunit: line 3: declare: -g: invalid option

Your system bash is too old. AceUnit requires bash 5, ksh, or zsh.

Fix on macOS: Run ./configure.sh to switch aceunit to zsh, or install bash 5:

brew install bash

Fix on other systems: Install bash 5 or ensure ksh or zsh is on your PATH.

docs.title: objdump: command not found on FreeBSD / BSD
docs.text:
objdump is not installed by default on BSD systems.

Option 1: Install binutils:

pkg install binutils       # FreeBSD
pkg_add binutils           # OpenBSD

Option 2: Use nm instead:

aceunit -t nm *_test.o >testcases.c

docs.title: My test functions are not discovered
docs.text:
Check that:

  1. Function names start with test (lowercase): testFoo, testBar
  2. Functions are compiled into the object file you passed to aceunit
  3. Functions have external linkage (not static)
  4. If using a custom prefix, you passed -p PREFIX to aceunit

Verify symbols are present:

nm leapyear_test.o | grep test

docs.title: Using a custom prefix
docs.text:
If your project uses a module prefix like HeapTest_:

aceunit -p 'HeapTest_' heap_test.o >testcases.c

AceUnit will discover functions like HeapTest_beforeAll, HeapTest_testAllocate, etc.

docs.title: Tests stop at first failure
docs.text:
You are probably using SimpleRunner. Switch to a runner that continues after failure:

  • For POSIX hosts: link with -laceunit-fork
  • For embedded: link with -laceunit-setjmp
  • For Windows/non-POSIX hosts: link with -laceunit-abort

See Runners.

docs.title: SIGSEGV crashes the test runner
docs.text: Use ForkRunner (-laceunit-fork). It runs each test case in a child process, so a crash terminates the child but not the runner. Other runners do not catch signals.

docs.title: Linking with a program that has its own main()
docs.text:
Use __wrap_main() and link with --wrap=main:

cc *.o testcases.o -laceunit-fork -Wl,--wrap=main -o tests

See __wrap_main() in the API reference.

docs.title: How do I test a function that calls puts() or other I/O?
docs.text: See the Hello World examples — five different approaches to mocking or intercepting I/O side effects.

docs.title: Can I use <assert.h> instead of <aceunit.h>?
docs.text: Yes, with AbortRunner or ForkRunner. The system assert() calls abort(), which both of those runners handle. SetJmpRunner and SimpleRunner will not catch it correctly — use <aceunit.h> with those.

docs.title: How do I install AceUnit into my project (not system-wide)?
docs.text:
make install PREFIX=/path/to/myproject/third_party/aceunit

Then in your Makefile:

ACEUNIT_HOME=/path/to/myproject/third_party/aceunit
ACEUNIT=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/bin/aceunit
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/lib/libaceunit-fork.a
CPPFLAGS+=-I$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/include

docs.title: Multiple fixtures — how do I combine them?
docs.text:
Pass all test object files to aceunit at once:

aceunit module1_test.o module2_test.o >testcases.c

testcases.c will contain a fixture entry for each object file.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide gets you from zero to a passing test suite in about 5 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• bash 5, ksh, or zsh
  • GNU make 3.81 or newer (often gmake on BSD)
  • A C compiler (gcc, clang, or similar)
  • objdump, readelf, or nm (usually part of binutils)

macOS

/bin/bash on macOS is very old. Run ./configure.sh to switch aceunit to zsh, or install a newer bash via Homebrew.

docs.title: Step 1: Build and Install AceUnit
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/christianhujer/aceunit
cd aceunit
make
sudo make install          # installs to /usr/local/

To install elsewhere:

sudo make install PREFIX=/opt/aceunit/

docs.title: Step 2: Write a Module
docs.text:
Create the module you want to test.

leapyear.h
#ifndef LEAPYEAR_H
#define LEAPYEAR_H
#include <stdbool.h>
extern bool isLeapYear(int year);
#endif
leapyear.c
#include "leapyear.h"

bool isLeapYear(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

docs.title: Step 3: Write Tests
docs.text:
Name your test functions starting with test. No registration needed.

leapyear_test.c
#include "leapyear.h"
#include <assert.h>

void testLeapYears(void) {
    assert(isLeapYear(0));
    assert(isLeapYear(4));
    assert(isLeapYear(400));
}

void testNonLeapYears(void) {
    assert(!isLeapYear(1));
    assert(!isLeapYear(100));
}

docs.title: Step 4: Build and Run
docs.text:
# Compile
cc -c leapyear.c
cc -c leapyear_test.c

# Generate fixture table from object files
aceunit leapyear_test.o >testcases.c

# Compile fixture table
cc -c testcases.c

# Link with AceUnit runner
cc leapyear.o leapyear_test.o testcases.o -laceunit-fork -o leapyear_test

# Run
./leapyear_test

Expected output:

AceUnit: 2 test cases, 2 successful, 0 failed.

docs.title: Step 5: Add a Makefile
docs.text:
Makefile
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY=-laceunit-fork
CPPFLAGS+=-W -Wall -pedantic

.PHONY: all
all: test

leapyear_test: leapyear.o leapyear_test.o testcases.o
    $(CC) $^ $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY) -o $@

testcases.c: leapyear_test.o
    aceunit $^ >$@

.PHONY: test
test: leapyear_test
    ./$^

.PHONY: clean
clean:
    $(RM) *.o leapyear_test testcases.c

Now just run make to build and test.

docs.text:

  • Choose the right runner for your environment
  • See the complete leapyear example with explanations

docs.title: Makefile Integration
docs.text: AceUnit is designed to integrate naturally with GNU Make. This page shows common patterns.

docs.title: Minimal Makefile
docs.text:
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY=-laceunit-fork
CPPFLAGS+=-W -Wall -pedantic

.PHONY: all
all: test

leapyear_test: leapyear.o leapyear_test.o testcases.o
    $(CC) $^ $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY) -o $@

testcases.c: leapyear_test.o
    aceunit $^ >$@

.PHONY: test
test: leapyear_test
    ./$^

.PHONY: clean
clean:
    $(RM) *.o leapyear_test testcases.c

docs.title: Using aceunit.mk
docs.text:
AceUnit ships with include/aceunit.mk which provides reusable variables and patterns. After installation it is available at $(PREFIX)/include/aceunit.mk.

include /usr/local/include/aceunit.mk

CPPFLAGS+=-W -Wall -pedantic
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY=$(ACEUNIT_SETJMP_LIBRARY)   # or FORK, ABORT, SIMPLE

.PHONY: all
all: test

mymodule_test: mymodule.o mymodule_test.o testcases.o $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY)

testcases.c: mymodule_test.o
    $(ACEUNIT) $^ >$@

.PHONY: test
test: mymodule_test
    ./$^

docs.title: Bundled AceUnit (in-project)
docs.text:
When AceUnit is not installed system-wide, point ACEUNIT_HOME at the source tree:

ACEUNIT_HOME=../../aceunit
ACEUNIT=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/bin/aceunit
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/lib/libaceunit-fork.a
CPPFLAGS+=-I$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/include

.PHONY: all
all: test

mymodule_test: mymodule.o mymodule_test.o testcases.o $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY)

$(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY):
    $(MAKE) -C $(ACEUNIT_HOME)/lib

testcases.c: mymodule_test.o
    $(ACEUNIT) $^ >$@

.PHONY: test
test: mymodule_test
    ./$^

.PHONY: clean
clean:
    $(RM) *.o mymodule_test testcases.c

docs.title: Multiple Fixtures
docs.text:
When you have many test object files, use pattern rules and patsubst:

ACEUNIT_HOME=../../aceunit
ACEUNIT=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/bin/aceunit
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/lib/libaceunit-fork.a
CPPFLAGS+=-I$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/include

sources=$(wildcard *.c)
objects=$(patsubst %.c,%.o,$(sources))
test_objects=$(filter %_test.o,$(objects))
prod_objects=$(filter-out %_test.o,$(objects))

testcases.c: $(test_objects)
    $(ACEUNIT) $^ >$@

unittest: $(prod_objects) $(test_objects) testcases.o $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY)

.PHONY: test
test: unittest
    ./unittest

docs.title: Recursive Builds
docs.text: For projects with multiple subdirectories, AceUnit provides recurse.mk. See recurse.mk in the repository root for details.

docs.title: Cross-Compilation
docs.text: See Cross-Compilation for how to use AceUnit with different compilers and target architectures in the same build.

docs.title: Migration Guide
docs.text: This guide helps users of AceUnit v1 and v2 migrate to v3.

docs.title: Generator
docs.text: v1 / v2 v3 Generator Java program parsing source files Shell script reading object file symbol tables Discovery Fake annotations (A_Test, A_Before, etc.) Naming convention (test*, beforeEach, etc.) Dependency Java runtime required bash/ksh/zsh + nm/objdump/readelf

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: v1 / v2 v3 A_Before beforeEach A_BeforeClass beforeAll A_After afterEach A_AfterClass afterAll A_Test test prefix (no annotation)

docs.title: Runner
docs.text:
v3 has a modular runner. Choose by linking against the appropriate library:

  • libaceunit-simple.a
  • libaceunit-setjmp.a
  • libaceunit-abort.a
  • libaceunit-fork.a

docs.title: Template
docs.text: v1/v2 used JUnit 4 as the template. v3 is modelled after JUnit 5.

docs.title: Step 1: Rename Lifecycle Functions
docs.text:
Rename functions in all test files:

Find Replace with Functions annotated A_Before Rename to beforeEach Functions annotated A_BeforeClass Rename to beforeAll Functions annotated A_After Rename to afterEach Functions annotated A_AfterClass Rename to afterAll Functions annotated A_Test Add test prefix

You do not need to remove the old annotations at this stage. After renaming, both v2 and v3 can run the tests in parallel — which is useful for a gradual migration.

docs.title: Step 2: Install v3
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/christianhujer/aceunit
cd aceunit
make
sudo make install

docs.title: Step 3: Run Tests with v3
docs.text: Point your build at the v3 aceunit binary and one of the new libraries. Verify all tests still pass.

docs.title: Step 4: Remove Old Annotations
docs.text: Once v3 is working, remove the old A_Test, A_Before, etc. annotations from your test files. They are no longer needed or parsed.

docs.title: Step 5: Deactivate v2
docs.text: Remove the v2 aceunit binary and library from your build.

docs.title: Benefits of Migrating
docs.text:
• Shell script is less fragile than Java source parsing — renames and comments no longer confuse the generator
  • No Java runtime required in the build environment
  • Modular runner lets you use ForkRunner on developer machines and SetJmpRunner on the target
  • Active maintenance — v2 is EOL

docs.title: Tested Compilers

docs.title: macOS Notes
docs.text:
The system bash on macOS (/bin/bash) is extremely old and does not support constructs used by aceunit. Fix this in one of two ways:

  1. Run ./configure.sh — automatically detects your OS and patches bin/aceunit to use zsh
  2. Install bash 5 via Homebrew — brew install bash

docs.title: FreeBSD Notes
docs.text:
objdump is not installed by default on FreeBSD. Install binutils:

pkg install binutils

Alternatively, use -t nm or -t readelf when calling aceunit.

docs.title: Cross-Compilation
docs.text: See Cross-Compilation for details on building and testing across multiple targets.

docs.title: Example: Hello World
docs.text:
Unit-testing hello, world! sounds trivial but poses real challenges:

  1. The program has a main() function — which conflicts with the test runner's main()
  2. puts() is a side-effect — the test must intercept or mock it

AceUnit includes five examples that solve these challenges in different ways. Source: examples/hello_world_*/ in the repository.

docs.title: The Program Under Test
docs.text:
All five examples test this same program:

hello.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    puts("Hello, world!");
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

docs.title: Variant 1: hello_world_mocked_macro
docs.text:
How: Compile-time macros redirect main and puts to different names.

  • -Dmain=original_main renames main at compile time
  • -Dputs=mocked_puts redirects puts to a mock at compile time

Pros: Simple, portable, no objcopy needed Cons: Requires recompiling the source with special flags (not always possible)

hello_test.c
#include "mock_puts.h"

extern int original_main(void);

void test_hello(void) {
    original_main();
    assert_puts("Hello, world!\n");
}

docs.title: Variant 2: hello_world_mocked_obj
docs.text:
How: objcopy renames symbols in the compiled object file.

  • main → original_main
  • puts → mocked_puts

The mock provides mocked_puts (collects output into a buffer) and assert_puts (verifies the buffer).

Pros: No source modification needed; works on pre-compiled objects Cons: Requires GNU objcopy

docs.title: Variant 3: hello_world_mocked_link
docs.text:
How: GNU linker --wrap feature redirects puts at link time.

  • hello.o is processed with objcopy to rename main → real_main
  • puts is redirected to __wrap_puts via -Wl,--wrap=puts

Pros: No source modification; linker-level interception Cons: GNU/Clang toolchain only; does not work on macOS (Darwin linker)

docs.title: Variant 4: hello_world_mocked_interpose
docs.text:
How: Darwin/macOS DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES interposer overrides puts at runtime.

  • main renamed with objcopy/llvm-objcopy
  • puts intercepted at runtime via dyld interposer

Pros: macOS-native approach; no source changes Cons: macOS only; requires llvm-objcopy

Finding llvm-objcopy on macOS

If llvm-objcopy is not found, check where LLVM is installed: 

export PATH=$(brew --prefix llvm)/bin:$PATH

docs.title: Variant 5: hello_world_intercepted_obj
docs.text:
How: Intercepts stdout/stderr using a pipe instead of mocking puts.

  • main renamed with objcopy
  • Test redirects stdout before calling original_main(), reads the output, asserts it

Pros: No mock needed; tests real I/O behavior Cons: More complex test code; pipe setup required

docs.title: Choosing a Variant
docs.text:
Variant Portability Source changes needed Toolchain requirement mocked_macro High Yes (recompile with flags) Any C compiler mocked_obj Medium No GNU objcopy mocked_link Medium No GNU/Clang linker mocked_interpose Low (macOS) No LLVM + Darwin loader intercepted_obj Medium No GNU objcopy

For most Linux/embedded projects, mocked_obj or mocked_macro is the pragmatic choice.

docs.title: Example: Leap Year
docs.text:
The leap year example is the simplest possible AceUnit project: a pure, side-effect-free function tested with no mocking needed.

Source: examples/leapyear/ in the repository.

docs.title: The Module Under Test
The Tests
The Makefile
docs.text:
Makefile
ACEUNIT_HOME=../..
ACEUNIT:=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/bin/aceunit
CPPFLAGS:=-W -Wall -pedantic -I$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/include
ACEUNIT_LIBRARY:=$(ACEUNIT_HOME)/lib/libaceunit-fork.a

.PHONY: all
all: test

leapyear_test: leapyear_test.o leapyear.o testcases.o $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY)

.PHONY: test
test: leapyear_test
    ./$^

testcases.c: leapyear_test.o
    $(ACEUNIT) $(ACEUNIT_FLAGS) $^ >$@

.PHONY: clean
clean::
    $(RM) *.[adios] leapyear_test testcases.c

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
cd examples/leapyear
make

Expected output:

AceUnit: 2 test cases, 2 successful, 0 failed.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Test functions need no registration — just name them test*
  • You can use <assert.h> directly (with ForkRunner or AbortRunner)
  • testcases.c is auto-generated; never edit it manually
  • The $(ACEUNIT_LIBRARY) dependency ensures AceUnit is built before the test

docs.title: Runners
docs.text: A runner is the part of AceUnit that calls test functions and handles failures. You select a runner by linking against the corresponding static library.

docs.title: Which Runner Should I Use?
docs.text:
Are you on a freestanding / bare-metal environment?
├─ Yes → Does your environment provide <setjmp.h>?
│        ├─ Yes → SetJmpRunner  (libaceunit-setjmp.a)
│        └─ No  → SimpleRunner  (libaceunit-simple.a)
└─ No (hosted) → Does your OS support fork()?
                 ├─ Yes (Linux, macOS, BSD, etc.) → ForkRunner   (libaceunit-fork.a)
                 └─ No  (Windows, AmigaOS, DOS)  → AbortRunner  (libaceunit-abort.a)

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Runner Library Continues after fail Catches SIGABRT Catches SIGSEGV Requires POSIX Simple libaceunit-simple.a ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ SetJmp libaceunit-setjmp.a ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ Abort libaceunit-abort.a ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ (needs signal()) Fork libaceunit-fork.a ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓

docs.title: Detailed Guides
docs.text:
• SimpleRunner
  • SetJmpRunner
  • AbortRunner
  • ForkRunner

docs.title: AbortRunner
docs.text:
Library: libaceunit-abort.a

The AbortRunner extends SetJmpRunner with a SIGABRT signal handler. When a test case calls abort() (including through the system's <assert.h>), the signal handler performs a longjmp() back to the runner.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Hosted environments without POSIX fork(): Windows, AmigaOS, MS-DOS
  • When you want to use the system's <assert.h> and its output format
  • Good general-purpose choice for hosted non-POSIX development

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
runner installs SIGABRT handler, calls setjmp()
  → calls test case
    → assert() from <assert.h> fails → abort() → SIGABRT
    → signal handler performs longjmp() back to runner
  → runner marks test failed, restores signal handler, moves to next test case

docs.title: Assertion Compatibility
docs.text:
Works with:

  • <aceunit.h> assert() — calls AceUnit_fail() → abort() → caught
  • <assert.h> assert() — calls abort() → caught
  • <stdlib.h> abort() — caught

Does not work with:

  • <stdlib.h> exit() — not a signal; process exits
  • Signals other than SIGABRT (like SIGSEGV)

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
cc *.o testcases.o -laceunit-abort -o tests

LOADLIBES=-laceunit-abort

docs.title: ForkRunner
docs.text:
Library: libaceunit-fork.a

The ForkRunner executes each test function in a separate child process using POSIX fork(). A test is marked failed if the child process exits with a non-zero status or is terminated by a signal.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• POSIX environments: Linux, macOS, BSD, Haiku, Solaris
  • Best isolation: a SIGSEGV in a test does not crash the runner
  • When you want to detect crashes, infinite loops (with timeout), or calls to exit()

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
for each fixture function:
  fork() → child runs the function
  parent waits for child
  if child exited != 0 or killed by signal → mark failed

docs.title: Assertion Compatibility
docs.text:
Works with everything:

  • <aceunit.h> assert() ✓
  • <assert.h> assert() ✓
  • <stdlib.h> abort() ✓
  • <stdlib.h> exit() ✓
  • Abnormal termination (SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, etc.) ✓

Does not need or use longjmp() — the child process provides isolation.

docs.title: Note on longjmp()
docs.text: The ForkRunner does not support longjmp() as an assertion mechanism — and there is no need to. longjmp() exists in other runners as a workaround for lacking process isolation. With fork(), that isolation is native.

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
cc *.o testcases.o -laceunit-fork -o tests

LOADLIBES=-laceunit-fork

docs.title: SetJmpRunner
docs.text:
Library: libaceunit-setjmp.a

The SetJmpRunner wraps each test case with setjmp()/longjmp(). When a test case calls AceUnit_fail(), it performs a longjmp() back to the runner, which marks the test failed and continues to the next one.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Embedded / freestanding environments that provide <setjmp.h>
  • Any environment without POSIX fork()
  • The default choice for embedded development

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
runner calls setjmp()
  → calls test case
    → test fails → AceUnit_fail() → longjmp() back to runner
  → runner marks test failed, moves to next test case

docs.title: Assertion Compatibility
docs.text:
Works with:

  • <aceunit.h> assert() — the primary choice; calls AceUnit_fail() → longjmp()
  • <setjmp.h> longjmp() — directly supported

Does not work with:

  • <assert.h> assert() — calls abort(), not longjmp(); will terminate the process
  • Signals (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT)

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
cc *.o testcases.o -laceunit-setjmp -o tests

LOADLIBES=-laceunit-setjmp

docs.title: SimpleRunner
docs.text:
Library: libaceunit-simple.a

The SimpleRunner executes test cases without any error interception. If a test case fails (via AceUnit_fail()), which internally calls abort(), execution stops immediately.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Learning TDD for the first time
  • Environments with no <setjmp.h> and no POSIX
  • Quick prototyping where stopping on first failure is acceptable

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Stops at the first failure — no summary of total test count vs. failures
  • Does not catch SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, or any other signal
  • Not suitable for production CI where you want full failure reports

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
cc *.o testcases.o -laceunit-simple -o tests

LOADLIBES=-laceunit-simple
